courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.content: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.content: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.content: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.content: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.

contributions.contribution: examines how institutions, participation and policy shape collective sustainability decisions

courses.name: Conservation Biology
courses.content: There have been many extinction events in earth’s history, including 5 mass extinctions, where at least 70% of species have died out. These have all been the result of global changes in climate and habitat, due to large catastrophic events or major shifts in atmospheric composition. We are currently on the cusp of a 6th mass extinction, the Holocene mass extinction. However, this one is caused by the actions of a single species: Homo sapiens. Our actions have both directly (overhunting/fishing) or indirectly (climate change, habitat destruction) caused many species to already go extinct, and brought thousands, if not millions, more to the brink of extinction. While we can not (or should not) bring back those species already lost, and many others will likely be lost before we have a chance to save them, we are capable of saving many more. This is the work of Conservation Biologists the world over. In this course we will explore both the causes and effects of our impact on the planet, as well as what action can and are being taken to reduce the loss in biodiversity as much as possible. We will look at current research, projects, but also legislation, aimed at saving as much of our planets biosphere as we can.

contributions.contribution: examines biodiversity loss, conservation strategies and the interaction between ecological evidence and human choices

courses.name: The Science of Evolution
courses.content: The theory of evolution was contentious when it was first proposed by Darwin and Wallace in the 19th century. The human-centric view of the world would be replaced by the idea that random changes created everything in the world around us, including ourselves, something that did not quite sit right with society at large. Even today, there are many people in the world that do not believe that evolution explains our planet’s state of being. As the principles of evolution can be applied to any and all aspects, understanding how it has affected, and still affects, the world might very well be the most important part of any study in biology. In this course we will explore the topic of evolution from different angles and at different levels, from genes to populations, and cover the basics for all relevant aspects with regard to life on this planet. From the history through the mechanisms, we will familiarize ourselves with both the theoretical as well as the practical study of evolution, and gain an understanding of how we got here ourselves.

contributions.contribution: provides evolutionary explanations for biological variation, adaptation and human health

courses.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
courses.content: Ecology is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine distribution and abundance. Over the past decades, ecology has grown from an obscure science into a position at the forefront of public and political consciousness. Applied ecology has become an important scientific tool to address important political and environmental issues. Ecology is generally divided into 3 levels: the individual organism, the population (consisting of individuals of the same species) and the community, in which several species are living together. In addition, ecology focuses on the relationship between living creatures and their chemical and physical surroundings, which together make up an ecosystem. Ecology is a complex science. It draws on many areas of knowledge such as organic and inorganic chemistry, plant and animal biology, physiology, meteorology, and even economics. This course focuses on the basic principles of ecology, from individuals to ecosystems. We then proceed to environmental conditions and resources, and the 4 levels of ecology: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Two weeks will be spent on ecological modelling, as an important tool for understanding and predicting ecological systems. We will conclude with some actual cases of applied ecology.

contributions.contribution: develops ecological understanding of organisms, populations, communities and ecosystems

courses.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
courses.content: The production of food is a contentious topic in our modern society. Current farming methods are major contributors to environmental harm worldwide. However, the human population is expected to continue to grow to 10 billion before peaking, with the greatest growth forecast in developing countries. Sustainable farming is the approach where both food needs and environmental impact are balanced. As current farming practices are generally more concerned about output than impact, change is necessary to ensure a sustainable future, while still ensuring the human population can be fed adequately. In this course we will learn about and discuss different aspects of farming that contribute to future plans and directions of sustainable farming on a global scale. Current practices and environmental impacts will be presented, to understand where we are starting from. Current alternatives will be critically assessed, to understand how we might progress. Innovations and modern approaches will be researched, to understand where we might end up. The purpose of this course is not to convince you of what the right way forward is, but to present information objectively, so that you can make up your own mind and help build a more sustainable future.

contributions.contribution: connects agroecology, food production and technological innovation in sustainable farming systems

courses.name: Law, Society & Justice
courses.content: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.

courses.name: Modern History
courses.content: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.

courses.name: Histories of Gender
courses.content: This course explores the histories and lives of children and young and older adults, through the lens of gender within an American context. The education takes place in a safe environment where critical thought thrives. The time frame is the 19th through the 21st centuries. Thematic topics unfold within a chronological framework. They include slavery in the nineteenth century, surviving and thriving in the twentieth century, and individual and community activism today. The approach centers storytelling. Throughout the term we explore the significance of the ways gendered stories are told by i.e., educational institutions, in children’s storybooks, within the medical community, across social media, through cultural expressions and forms, and by individual people. For instance, class members conduct interviews of elderly Queer folks and interpret their findings by drawing from scholars including bell hooks and Kimberle Crenshaw. They also contribute to the semester long Walking with Pride Project, an activist artwork woven by students, Queer and multiply marginalized people world-wide, and their allies. The rug features digitally in https://thewalkingwithprideproject.wordpress.com/, and physically in cultural spaces internationally. Finally, students explore repression, resistance, and/or retribution in their final project, where they choose both the content of their research, ranging from transphobia to banned books, as well as the form, including but not limited to, an essay, podcast, graphic novel, or artistic expression.

contributions.contribution: uses gender as a historical category to analyse institutions, inequality and social change

courses.name: History Research Seminar
courses.content: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.

courses.name: Introduction to Public International Law
courses.content: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.

contributions.contribution: develops public-international-law analysis of states, institutions, rights and cross-border obligations

courses.name: Principles of Private Law
courses.content: Life comprises a variety of situations in which private law plays a role . Simply considering the home implicates several complex relationships: family relatives , landlords and tenants, neighbors. Stepping out the front door leads to a further range of transactions that can have legal consequences for those involved. The rights and obligations associated with relationships and transactions among (natural and legal) persons are largely determined by a collection of legal areas known collectively as private law. This course introduces students to principles of selected fields of private law, and students will closely examine property law, tort law, contract law, and other legal areas. The overarching principles within each of these fields will be illuminated using a comparative law approach, considering primarily the legal systems of Germany, France, England, China, and the United States of America. Additionally, students will be challenged to consider private law concepts in broader contexts. Building on the skills acquired in GOSLAWJ101 and other UCR law track courses , this course on private law will seek to uncover the latent social, economic, and political pressures underlying many of the legal principles that will be discussed.

courses.name: Foundations of European Union Law
courses.content: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.

courses.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courses.content: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives.

contributions.contribution: provides philosophical foundations for analysing knowledge, reality, ethics and human life

courses.name: Ethics
courses.content: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.

contributions.contribution: develops normative reasoning about moral problems, responsibility and competing principles

courses.name: Philosophy of Emotion
courses.content: Emotions are a basic aspect of human experience, but they have been, throughout the history of philosophy, contrasted with and sidelined by the pursuit of rationality. They seem to be of important value, central to our well-being, and yet they can often be deeply messy and puzzling. This course provides the opportunity to engage with key questions in the study of emotions from a philosophical perspective. The core topics we shall explore in the course are: (i) The nature of emotions. What are emotions? Are they like beliefs, feelings, or perceptions? (ii) Emotions and ethics. What is the role of emotion in well-being? How important are emotions for moral judgment? In what ways are emotions significant for moral motivation and character? (iii) Emotions and rationality. What does it mean for an emotion to be appropriate? What makes emotions rational or irrational? (iv) Particular emotions: love, fear, disgust; emotions and moods. (v) Emotions and politics. What is the place of the emotions in the context of political projects? Are there emotions we should cultivate as a political community, others we should reject? (vi) Emotions and art. Are we able to experience genuine emotion towards works of fiction? Are there emotions that are specific to the appreciation of art? What is the relation between aesthetic emotions and moral emotions? GOSPHIL311: Philosophy of Emotion We will consider sources from the history of philosophy as well contemporary research on the emotions from philosophy and additional disciplines.

contributions.contribution: connects philosophical analysis of emotion with questions about mind, agency and human experience

courses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courses.content: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.

courses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courses.content: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.

courses.name: Theory of International Relations
courses.content: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.

courses.name: European Union Politics
courses.content: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.

courses.name: Peace & Conflict
courses.content: Peace and Conflict Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the causes, consequences, and potential solutions to both violent and nonviolent conflicts. Its goal is to understand the complex factors that contribute to conflict, the dynamics of violence, and the strategies for achieving lasting peace. The field encompasses insights from history, sociology, political science, international relations, and law, among other disciplines . This course introduces the field by examining and assessing multi ple theories of conflict and peacebuilding in the context of ongoing and past conflicts at regional, national and international levels. Peace and Conflict Studies is not only interdisciplinary but also shaped by diverse analytical perspectives. Some approaches emphasize structural inequality , clashing ideologies, and others focus on humiliation, historical wounds, and identity -based grievances, particularly in colonial or postcolonial contexts. Each lens draws attention to different forms of evidence and different peacebuilding strategies. As a result, this course demonstrates the importance of adopting a holistic approach that includes in ternational, institutional, and state -led elements, as well as cultural, interpersonal, and bottom-up actions led by civil society. The course uses “Travelling Concepts” as a tool for critically applying an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will compare how “justice,” “truth,” or “reconciliation” are mobilized in legal vs.

courses.name: Introduction to Sociology
courses.content: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.content: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.

courses.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courses.content: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.

courses.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
courses.content: Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_ But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

courses.name: Pharmacology
courses.content: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.

courses.name: Infection & Immunity
courses.content: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.

courses.name: Mechanisms of Disease
courses.content: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. The aim of this course is to provide insight in the principles of the mechanisms of diseases. For the organ systems mentioned the student first has to study the embryology and anatomy, Using this information as starting point, the basic physiology is studied and using the combined knowledge the student must be able to derive the symptoms and failures in the system or the pathophysiology.

courses.name: Neurobiology
courses.content: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.

courses.name: Psycholinguistics
courses.content: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

courses.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courses.content: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.

courses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courses.content: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16

courses.name: Molecular Cell Biology
courses.content: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. The course consists of five themes: 1 – The fundamental units of life: Cellular components, chemistry and energetics 2 – Genomes: DNA to Proteins, replication, repair and regulation of gene expression 3 – Cellular dynamics: Membrane trafficking, transport and signaling pathways 4 – Cell fate: Cell division, tissues, stem cells and cancer 5 – Drug Mechanisms (Paper and Poster Project)

courses.name: Human Physiology
courses.content: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.

courses.name: Biochemistry
courses.content: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.

contributions.contribution: explains the molecular chemistry and metabolic processes that sustain living systems

courses.name: Life Science Laboratory
courses.content: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).

courses.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
courses.content: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.

courses.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courses.content: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.

courses.name: Abnormal Psychology
courses.content: The definition of what is a mental disorder is very complex, and there is no universal agreement about it. This course explores mental health and mental disorders across the lifespan, emphasizing a bio-psycho-social perspective that considers how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to promote mental health or contribute to the development of disorders. Students are introduced to historical and contemporary views of psychopathology, the prevalence and development of mental disorders, and the role of culture, gender, and environmental factors in shaping mental health and illness. The course familiarizes students with key concepts, terminology, theories, and research methods in psychopathology, while fostering critical thinking and analytical skills for evaluating mental health information. It addresses the assessment, diagnosis, classification, and treatment of mental disorders, including the most prevalent disorders from infancy through adulthood. Through interactive lectures, audiovisual materials, discussions, exercises, and written assignments, students gain a research-oriented understanding of maladaptive behavior and develop greater awareness of both their own mental health and the mental health of others within a comprehensive bio-psycho-social framework.

courses.name: Medical & Health Psychology
courses.content: In th is course, Medical and Health Psychology , we will examine the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and socio-cultural factors that influence health and illness. Guided by the core principle of the field, the bio-psycho-social approach of the human being, we will explore key theories, research findings, and specific interventions within clinical health psychology, with a particular focus on the role of psychological expertise and mental health professionals in medical settings. Based on the World Health Organization’s (1948) definition of Health as a state of physical, mental and social well-being with a special emphasis in the balance between these aspects , Health Psychology is concerned with the elements that influence health and illness across the individual lifespan. It considers the implication of multiple aspects that can be combined in a complex way to promote and maintain health or to contribute for the settlement of dysfunction or illness. Therefore, This course will provide stude nts with a comprehensive understanding of these determinants and factors by addressing the following core areas: 1) Attitudes, behavior and lifestyle factors affecting health and disease; 2) Stress and the related psychosocial factors and processes associated with disease development and progression; Course outline HCBPSYC311 Medical & Health Psychology Page 2 of 11 3) Biopsychosocial factors involved in the illness experience; as well as, the long -term social and psychological implications of chronic illness; 4) Relevance of psychological interventions in medical…

Ethical issues in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 2. Mental Health intervention processes: Psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 3. Clinical psychological assessment: Psychodiagnostics; 4. Psychological assessment in infants, children, adolescents and adults; 5. Clinical psychological interventions and treatments: Different approaches in psychotherapy; 6. Another objective of the course is to promote the development of critical thinking in the field of Clinical Psychology, especially in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies, to prepare the students to be cautious and analytical consumers of information on matters related to these topics.

courses.name: Advanced Research Seminar
courses.content: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.

courses.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
courses.content: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.

Focusing on major stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, the course lays the groundwork for advanced art history studies. It introduces essential tools for visual analysis and interpretation, fostering an understanding of how visual culture reflects historical contexts and societal values.

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
courses.content: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.

contributions.contribution: introduces close reading, literary interpretation and critical analysis of cultural texts

courses.name: Great Literary Works
courses.content: This course is based on a selection of major literary texts which should be considered essential for every LAS student’s cultural capital: texts that for centuries have inspired Western culture, visual arts and theatre, and which resonate themes that preoccupy social sciences and philosophy. The course is a chronological overview of literature ranging from the earliest monuments (the epic of Gilgamesh) to post-modernity. Within this framework students will read primary (literary) and secondary (critical, theoretical) texts debating what it means to be human, mortal, female, male, or child, or what it means to be responsible, free, a member of family or other community, to be civilized or barbarian. What makes literature different from anecdote? Why are some children’s texts indebted to philosophical tale? Probing these and many other questions, students will be invited to analyse literary representations of home, labour, leisure, duty, love, leadership, organized religion, and memory, and try to correlate these topics with various artistic forms used by writers. In this way the course is an encounter with diverse genres: heroic epic, philosophical tale, fairy tale, short story, autobiography, essay and novella. With this broad approach to themes and forms in the Western literary heritage, the course is an alternative introduction to literary studies, and of fundamental value to everyone interested in literary and cultural studies.

contributions.contribution: examines major literary works across periods and cultures through close reading and comparative interpretation

courses.name: Life & Travel Writing
courses.content: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts.

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.content: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.

courses.name: The Documentary
courses.content: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
